claims.text: The baseline FeNiCrCoCu coating has moderate phase separation and noticeable Cu-rich grain boundaries.
Increasing the quenching rate or applying an alternative thermal treatment can reduce Cu segregation at grain boundaries relative to the baseline coating.
At temperatures above approximately 500°C, diffusion and dislocation activity are significantly activated in the coating.
Cu-rich grain boundaries act as mechanically weak interfaces in FeNiCrCoCu.
Cu-rich grain boundaries facilitate grain-boundary sliding and dislocation slipping.
High Cu concentration at grain boundaries locally lowers the critical resolved shear stress.
Phase separation involving Cu-rich and Cu-depleted regions produces an uneven stress distribution.
Dislocation slipping and grain-boundary sliding are principal plastic-deformation mechanisms in phase-separated Co-Cr-Cu-Fe-Ni.
Reducing Cu segregation will produce a more uniform grain-boundary composition.
Reducing Cu segregation will improve grain-boundary mechanical cohesion.
Reducing Cu segregation will suppress grain-boundary sliding and dislocation activity during high-temperature sliding.
Suppressing grain-boundary sliding and dislocation activity will reduce sliding wear.
A coating with reduced Cu enrichment will have a lower wear rate than the baseline coating under otherwise identical high-temperature sliding conditions.
Cu-rich grain boundaries reduce the tensile strength and ductility of Co-Cr-Cu-Fe-Ni.
The predicted relationship should hold in a high-temperature regime where grain-boundary and dislocation processes are thermally activated.
Oxidation or other degradation mechanisms may dominate wear outside the proposed regime.
The cited evidence is based on molecular-dynamics simulations under uniaxial tensile loading rather than high-temperature sliding-wear experiments.
The transfer of the tensile-deformation mechanism to sliding wear and the influence of the coating-substrate interface remain experimentally unverified.
Failure to obtain a statistically significant reduction in both wear rate and microscopic deformation in the reduced-segregation coating would falsify the hypothesis.
